Supervisor: Dr. Neel Kanth Kundu . Co-supervisor: Dr. Ramniwas Meena . Adopted the Curty–Azuma–Lo (CAL) Protocol-3 asymptotic, collective-attack security model as the baseline. Derived a finite-order analytical Hermite-moment expansion in the Gaussian log-transmittance domain, combined with an exact Euler–Stirling transformation back to the physical transmittance domain. Derived a zero-fitted-parameter matched-asymptotic surrogate for the CAL error-rate and key-rate quantities, and validated the closed-form turbulence average against 2 × 10⁵-sample Monte Carlo across eleven operating points. t: QSAFire
x: Jun – Aug 2026 QSAFire Satellite-to-ground SNS-TF-QKD simulation package, built at the Scientific Analysis Group, Defence Research and Development Organisation. Python SNS-TF-QKD Orbits Monte Carlo Streamlit Independent Python package for sending-or-not-sending twin-field QKD (SNS-TF-QKD) over three channels: fiber, free-space optics with Gamma-Gamma turbulence, and a ground-to-satellite uplink. It implements the asymptotic key-rate formula of Wang, Yu and Hu (Phys. Rev. A 98, 062323). The protocol equations live in one module and are reused unchanged by every channel model, so no physics is duplicated. The satellite link is built in separable layers: WGS-84 geodesy and a solved sun-synchronous orbit, Rayleigh, aerosol and gas optical depth, a Hufnagel-Valley turbulence profile with the spherical-wave Rytov variance, and seasonal datasets for winter, summer and monsoon. Hardware and environment are modeled explicitly: Friis diffraction loss, Gaussian pointing jitter, a characterised avalanche photodiode, day and night background light, and weather-gated annual availability from rainy-day and fog climatology. t: Hardware-Assisted Post-Processing for SNS-TF-QKD
x: Jul – Nov 2026 Hardware-Assisted Post-Processing for SNS-TF-QKD B.Tech micro project with Aayush Gupta, Bharati Vidyapeeth’s College of Engineering. It extends the work begun in the SAG, DRDO internship. OptiSystem MATLAB Python Verilog FPGA A three-station SNS-TF-QKD link (Alice, Bob and an untrusted Charlie) modelled in OptiSystem, with the protocol decisions run as MATLAB co-simulation blocks and every station logging a window-synchronised CSV file. A Python pipeline over a 32,768-window run: basis separation, phase post-selection, decoy-state estimation and the secret key rate with 95% Wilson confidence intervals. The key rate on that dataset is negative (R = −0.166 per window), and it is traced to detector clicks that are uncorrelated with phase, not to the analysis code. All 19 counters match a Python reference model, and it synthesises to 627 flip-flops and 24 LUTs for a Xilinx 7-series target. Place-and-route and on-board execution are future work. t: QSAFire, a satellite SNS-TF-QKD simulator built layer by layer
x: How I built QSAFire during my internship at DRDO's Scientific Analysis Group, and why every stage of the link budget is checked against an outside reference. [qsafire, sns-tf-qkd, satellite-qkd, simulation] During my summer internship at the Scientific Analysis Group of the Defence Research and Development Organisation, I built a simulator that answers one question. How much secret key can a ground station share with a satellite, and how does that change with the sky, the hardware and the weather? The result is QSAFire , an open source Python package for sending or not sending twin field quantum key distribution (SNS TF QKD). This post explains how it is put together and what I would still improve. The project entry is on the Projects page, and the code is on GitHub. The protocol SNS TF QKD lets two distant parties send weak pulses to a middle station. Each party decides in every time window whether to send or not send, which tolerates a large misalignment error between the two arms. QSAFire implements the asymptotic key rate formula from Wang, Yu and Hu, Sending or not sending: Twin field quantum key distribution with large misalignment error , Phys. Rev. A 98, 062323 (2018). The package runs the same protocol over three kinds of channel: Channel What it models Fiber A standard telecom fiber point to point link Free space A near ground optical link with Gamma Gamma scintillation Ground to satellite An uplink to a sun synchronous satellite, from orbit to detector One copy of the physics The first rule I set was that the rate equations exist in exactly one place. The photon number weights, the gain and error model, the decoy state bounds and the key rate formula all live in a single module, src/engine.py . The fiber, free space and satellite models import them unchanged.

t: SateSim, a satellite link budget simulator with a dashboard
x: How SateSim turns an orbit and a ground station into SNR, BER, Doppler shift and elevation, with a dashboard, CSV export and a PDF report. [satesim, link-budget, satellite, python] SateSim answers a basic question in satellite communication. For a satellite passing over a ground station, how good is the radio link at every moment? It combines orbit propagation, an RF link budget and a dashboard, and it produces SNR, bit error rate, Doppler shift and elevation angle for each pass. This post explains how it is organised and what it leaves out. The entry on the Projects page has the short version, and the code is on GitHub. From an orbit to a link budget The pipeline has three steps, and each one feeds the next. 1. Where is the satellite? SGP4, run through Skyfield, propagates the orbit and gives the satellite's position and velocity relative to the ground station at each time step. 2. How strong is the signal? The range and elevation from step one go into a link budget. Free space path loss and the Friis transmission equation turn distance and frequency into received power, and the received power gives the signal to noise ratio. 3. How good is the link? The SNR is mapped to a bit error rate for BPSK or QPSK modulation. Doppler shift comes from the same geometry. It is the projection of the satellite's relative velocity onto the line of sight, scaled by the carrier frequency. Satellites below a minimum elevation angle are dropped, because a link close to the horizon is not usable. t: Simulating a decoy-state BB84 satellite constellation over India
x: How the simulator behind my Springer paper works, from Walker-Delta orbits to the key a station collects in a day, and what its numbers do and do not say. [bb84, satellite-qkd, constellation, simulation] How much quantum secure key could a small satellite constellation deliver to ground stations in India in one day? That question is behind my first author paper in the International Journal of Information Technology (Springer, 2025), and this post describes the simulator I wrote to answer it. The project entry is on the Projects page, and the code is on GitHub. What it simulates The simulator follows a Walker Delta constellation of low Earth orbit satellites for 24 hours. For each satellite and ground station it finds when the satellite is visible, estimates the optical link loss, and computes the secret key rate and error rate of the decoy state BB84 protocol. The output is a set of per station CSV files, nine kinds of figure, and a dashboard for exploring the parameters. The default case has 3 orbital planes with 4 satellites each, at 600 km altitude and 97.5 degrees inclination, stepped every 5 minutes. The pieces Constellation. A Walker Delta generator builds the constellation from the usual T/P/F description and can export synthetic TLEs. The propagator is written in plain Python with no orbital library. It solves Kepler's equation by Newton Raphson and adds the J2 secular drift of the orbit plane: dot{ Omega} = tfrac{3}{2} , J 2 left( frac{R e}{p} right)^2 n cos i Positions go through the chain from orbital elements to ECI, then ECEF, then a local topocentric frame at the station. t: VeriSure AI, asking plain questions of insurance policies
x: How a hackathon prototype turns uploaded policy documents into a question-answering tool that cites the clauses behind each answer. [verisure-ai, rag, faiss, gemini] Insurance policies are long, and the answer to a simple question such as "is cataract surgery covered?" sits in one clause on page 31. VeriSure AI is a prototype I built for the HackRx 6.0 problem statement from the Bajaj Finserv Hackathon. You upload one or more policy documents, ask a question in plain language, and get back a structured decision with the clauses it relied on. The entry on the Projects page has the short version, and the code is on GitHub. The idea in one paragraph A language model should not be asked to read a whole policy and answer from memory. Instead, the system first finds the few clauses that matter for the question, and then asks the model to decide using only those clauses. This pattern is usually called retrieval augmented generation. It keeps the model's answer tied to text the user can check. How a question travels through it 1. Upload. The /upload docs endpoint accepts PDF and DOCX files, extracts their text and splits it into chunks. 2. Embed and index. Each chunk is turned into a vector with a MiniLM sentence transformer, and the vectors go into a FAISS index saved in a folder for that session. 3. Retrieve. The /query endpoint takes the question and the session ID, embeds the question, and pulls the most similar clauses from that session's index. 4. Decide. The clauses and the question go to Gemini 1.5 Flash, which replies with a JSON object. t: VibeSense, finding the products and the vibe in a short video
x: How a hackathon backend finds clothing items in a reel, matches them to a product catalog and names the aesthetic of the look. [vibesense, computer-vision, clip, faiss] Fashion now spreads through short videos. A viewer sees a look in a reel and wants two things: where to buy the pieces, and what the style is called. VibeSense is the backend engine I built for the Flickd AI Hackathon 2025 to answer both. Give it a short video and a caption, and it returns the products it recognises and the vibes the look carries, such as Coquette, Streetwear or Vintage. The entry on the Projects page has the short version, and the code is on GitHub. Two questions, two paths The system treats the picture and the caption separately and joins them at the end. What is being worn? Frames are pulled from the video with FFmpeg. A YOLOv8n detector finds clothing in each frame, and each detected item is cropped out. A CLIP model turns every crop into an embedding, and FAISS searches a pre built catalog of product images for the closest matches by cosine similarity. What is the style? The caption is read from a text file with the same name as the video. A sentence transformer embeds it and compares it with a list of vibe descriptions, which gives the vibe tags. The models, and why Stage Model Role Detection YOLOv8n Fast detection and cropping of clothing items Image embedding CLIP ViT B/32 Semantic image vectors for visual similarity Text embedding all MiniLM L6 v2 Compact vectors for captions and product text Matching FAISS, cosine similarity Nearest products across the catalog YOLOv8n was trained on the Fashionpedia dataset, which has 45 clothing categories with detailed annotations. The training notebook is in the repository. I chose small models on purpose: the goal was a lightweight pipeline

The idea is to help someone keep a loved one's way of speaking: you upload messages, photos and voice notes, and the system builds a chatbot that answers in that person's style. The entry on the Projects page has the short version, and the code is on GitHub. What goes in The system accepts three kinds of material about one person: Text , such as chat exports, and screenshots of messages that are read with Tesseract OCR Voice recordings , which Whisper turns into text Photos , used to build a visual profile Everything is converted to text or features, because the chatbot works from language. From material to persona My part was the analysis that sits between the raw files and the chatbot. 1. Extraction. OCR and transcription turn images and audio into text, alongside the text that was uploaded directly. 2. Personality analysis. The text is analysed for emotional tone, vocabulary and common phrases, so the persona has a recognisable voice. 3. Visual profile. Face detection and landmark checks, using the face recognition library and OpenCV, assess the uploaded photos. 4. Chatbot. A GPT style model, with OpenAI, DeepSeek or Gemini as the options, is prompted with the extracted profile and answers in character. 5. Portraits. Stable Diffusion can generate a portrait from a name and a style. Profiles and chat history are stored in SQLite, and a profile can be exported as a JSON file. The stack Part Technology I

t: Classifying paddy stress from 48 hours of weather, and testing it on a place it has never seen
x: A BiLSTM-LSTM model for three-class paddy stress, built with physiology-based labels and tested by holding out an entire coastal location. [paddy, lstm, agri-ai, domain-shift] Rice is sensitive to short spells of heat, dry air and high evaporative demand, and farmers decide on irrigation on exactly that timescale. This post describes a course project for CMU 11 785 (Introduction to Deep Learning) in which I built a model that reads 48 hours of weather and labels the stress on the crop as low, medium or high. The harder part was not the model. It was asking whether it still works in a climate it was never trained on. The entry on the Projects page has the short version, the full write up is the project report (PDF), and the code is on GitHub. The data The weather is hourly, for January 2023 to December 2024, from six places chosen to cover very different rice growing climates: Location Climate Jorhat, Assam Humid subtropical Ludhiana, Punjab Semi arid Lucknow, Uttar Pradesh Subhumid Kolkata, West Bengal Humid coastal monsoon Thanjavur, Tamil Nadu Tropical wet Visakhapatnam, Andhra Pradesh Coastal tropical With roughly 22,000–24,000 hourly samples per site, each hour is described by temperature, relative humidity, vapour pressure deficit (VPD, derived) and precipitation, together with short term gradients (change in temperature, RH and VPD), 6 to 12 hour rolling means, and derived indices (heat index and humidity ratio). These features emphasise the short term transitions that tend to come before stress. Soil moisture sensors were not available, so the model relies on weather driven atmospheric demand. t: Five months, one micro project, and Aayush
x: The part of my B.Tech micro project that isn't in the report: three reviews, an FPGA board that stayed in its box, and working with a partner who is never bothered by anything. [college, fpga, teamwork] Aayush and I just finished our B.Tech micro project, a hardware assisted post processing chain for SNS TF QKD (Aayush Gupta is my partner on it). The technical story is in that post and in the report. This one is about everything the report leaves out. Five months. Three reviews. And a plan that every single time ended with "and then we'll put it on the FPGA." We didn't. Diwali and the festive weeks came, the lab was shut right when we needed it, and the board never left its box. I'd love to blame only the calendar, but honestly, a good chunk of it was us. We kept saying "there's time" and then it was November. Classic. Working with Aayush is the best part of this whole project, and also the hardest. He's my Leonard. Calm, always up for the work, never bothered by anything. That's brilliant when a simulation crashes. It's less brilliant when I'm freaking out about a review and he just goes "yeah, it'll be fine." And it was fine. Every time. I still can't decide whether to be grateful or annoyed, so I'm both. And his calm isn't the peaceful kind. It's the "abhi time hai" kind. Every few days it went the same way. He'd ask, "micro karna hai?" I'd say, "haan, kar le." And he'd say, "rehne de, abhi time hai." :) Every. Single. Time. Always with a smile, never with a plan. The worst part is that I'd nod and agree, because honestly I wanted it to be true. We'd both walk away feeling very responsible for having had the conversation. t: Hardware-assisted post-processing for SNS-TF-QKD
x: My B.Tech micro project with Aayush Gupta. A three-station SNS-TF-QKD link in OptiSystem, a Python key-rate pipeline, and a Verilog sifter core that matches it on all 19 counters. The FPGA board run is still to do. [sns-tf-qkd, fpga, verilog, python, optisystem] This is the write up of my B.Tech micro project with Aayush Gupta. It grew out of the OptiSystem prototype I built during my DRDO internship, and asks a narrower question: the classical chain between a twin field QKD link and a key rate number is long, so which parts of it are really just counters, and could they live in an FPGA? This post is the technical side only. The full report, the slides and the poster are on the Publications page, and the code is in the snstfqkd fpga repository. The report has a DOI if you want to cite it: 10.5281/zenodo.24390550. The idea Between the physical protocol and a key rate plot sits window logging, basis sifting, phase post selection, decoy state estimation and finite count statistics. Mistakes in that chain corrupt the rate quietly: one CSV row per waveform sample instead of one per window, or Bob's inverted bit convention copied from Alice. The first half of the chain is nothing but comparisons and counters applied to a stream of windows. That is what FPGA fabric does well, and what a Python loop does one window at a time. The second half (ratios, logarithms, binary entropy) wants floating point, which the processing side of a PYNQ style Zynq board gives for free. So the plan was a split: counting in fabric, maths in Python. Stage 1: the link, in OptiSystem Three stations: Alice, Bob and an untrusted Charlie, joined by 40 km spans of SMF 28 at 0.2 dB/km (about 8 dB, a transmittance near 0.158). t: An SNS-TF-QKD link in OptiSystem, and the Python pipeline that reads its logs
x: How I built a physical-layer sending-or-not-sending twin-field QKD prototype in OptiSystem with MATLAB co-simulation, and the Python pipeline that turns its CSV logs into a key rate. [optisystem, sns-tf-qkd, matlab, python] My internship at the Scientific Analysis Group of the Defence Research and Development Organisation had two halves. The satellite half became QSAFire. The other half was smaller and more hands on: a 40 km fibre version of the same protocol, built at the level of lasers, modulators and detectors in OptiSystem, plus a Python pipeline that reads what that prototype logs. The two halves share no code, data or file format. This post covers the second half. Everything is in the osd folder of the QSAFIRE repository: the OptiSystem project files, the MATLAB blocks, the exported CSV logs and the post processing notebook, which also runs in Google Colab. The full description is in the internship report. The protocol, briefly In twin field QKD, Alice and Bob each send weak pulses to a middle station, Charlie, who interferes them on a beam splitter. A single click at one of Charlie's two detectors links their bits, and the key rate scales with the square root of the total channel transmittance, not with the full transmittance. That is how it gets past the limit for repeaterless point to point links. The original proposal had a gap. Its bit values were encoded in a global phase that has to be disclosed later, and Wang, Yu and Hu showed that this leaves room for an attack. Their sending or not sending (SNS) protocol removes the gap by changing where the bit comes from. t: Quantum Networks Under the Lens, Part 0: What does it take to build a global quantum network?
x: The opening of a short series of open questions from my work on satellite quantum communication, asked before any results. [quantum-networks, satellite-qkd, series] Over the past month, while working on a couple of research manuscripts in satellite quantum communications, I've found myself coming back to the same question again and again: What does it actually take to build a global quantum communication network? When people hear "quantum technology," the conversation usually revolves around quantum computers, algorithms, or cryptography. But once you start thinking about real world deployment, an entirely different set of challenges appears. Orbital mechanics. Atmospheric physics. Optical communication. Network scheduling. Constellation design. Operational efficiency. What surprised me most was how many seemingly straightforward assumptions become much less obvious when physics enters the picture. Does adding more satellites always help? Can geography matter more than hardware? Should networks be optimized for peak performance or long term stability? Over the next few weeks, I'll be sharing a short series called: "Quantum Networks Under the Lens" Five Questions Physics Still Hasn't Fully Answered These posts are inspired by questions I've been exploring while preparing upcoming manuscripts on satellite Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) and quantum communication networks. I won't be sharing results or conclusions yet. Just interesting questions, ideas, and discussions from the journey. Because sometimes the most valuable part of research isn't the answer...it's learning how to ask better questions. t: Quantum Networks Under the Lens, Part 1: Do more satellites always mean more throughput?
x: Adding satellites improves coverage, but does the useful key material grow at the same rate? A question from my work on large satellite QKD networks. [quantum-networks, satellite-qkd, series] At first glance, the answer seems obvious. More satellites should mean more coverage, more connectivity, and ultimately more secure key generation. Right? That's what I thought too. But the deeper I looked into satellite quantum communication networks, the more I realized that coverage and throughput aren't necessarily the same thing. Adding satellites can increase visibility and reduce coverage gaps. However, the amount of useful key material generated still depends on the quality of the optical links themselves. That raises an interesting question: If we keep adding satellites to a constellation, will throughput continue growing at the same rate? Or is there a point where coverage keeps improving while the throughput gains become smaller and smaller? It's a deceptively simple question, but physics rarely rewards simple intuition. I've been exploring this topic while preparing an upcoming manuscript on large scale satellite quantum communication networks. What would your intuition predict? t: Quantum Networks Under the Lens, Part 2: Is the atmosphere more important than the satellite?
x: Could the location of a ground station matter more than improvements in the communication hardware? A question about atmosphere and quantum links. [quantum-networks, atmosphere, series] When people think about satellite communication, the focus is usually on the satellite itself. The payload. The optics. The orbit. The technology onboard. But every photon still has to travel through something much closer to home: Earth's atmosphere. Turbulence. Humidity. Aerosols. Clouds. Seasonal weather patterns. All of these can influence how effectively an optical signal reaches a ground station. This led me to a question I hadn't thought much about before: Can the location of a ground station matter more than improvements in the communication hardware itself? In other words, if you had to choose between a better satellite and a better location, which would have the bigger impact? The answer isn't as obvious as it might seem. I've been exploring this intersection of atmospheric science and quantum communications while preparing one of my upcoming research manuscripts. What do you think? t: Quantum Networks Under the Lens, Part 3: Higher satellites or lower satellites?
x: Coverage and contact time favour high orbits, while path loss favours low ones. Which should a quantum network optimise for? [quantum-networks, satellite-qkd, series] Suppose you're designing a future quantum communication network. Would you place your satellites at 300 km or 1200 km altitude? At first glance, higher sounds better. More coverage Longer visibility windows Fewer coverage gaps But physics introduces a catch. As satellites move farther away, photons have to travel longer distances, and optical losses begin to grow. Lower orbits can provide: Stronger optical links Lower path loss Higher potential throughput Higher orbits can provide: Larger coverage footprints Better availability Longer contact times So which one should we optimize for? Availability or throughput? The interesting part is that improving one doesn't necessarily improve the other. Every design choice seems to solve one problem while creating a new one. I've been thinking a lot about this tradeoff while working on system level models for satellite Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) networks. If you were designing a global quantum communication network from scratch, where would you start? t: Quantum Networks Under the Lens, Part 4: Can stability be more valuable than performance?
x: A slightly slower network that is easier to operate can be the better one. A trade-off from working on large-scale satellite QKD. [quantum-networks, satellite-qkd, series] Engineers often optimize for maximum performance. But should they? Imagine two quantum communication networks. Network A Maximum possible throughput Constant switching between satellites Frequent tracking and control adjustments Network B Slightly lower throughput Fewer interruptions More stable operation Lower operational overhead Which network would you deploy? As satellite constellations become larger, another challenge starts to emerge: Handover management Tracking complexity Synchronization overhead Operational reliability Sometimes maximizing performance and maximizing practicality are not the same objective. In fact, a small sacrifice in throughput might significantly improve how efficiently a network can be operated. I've been exploring this tradeoff while working on large scale satellite Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) systems. Physics tells us what is possible. Engineering decides what is useful. t: Quantum Networks Under the Lens, Part 5: Can geography create quantum advantage?
x: Two identical systems in different places will not perform the same. Can geography become a strategic resource for quantum communication? [quantum-networks, atmosphere, series] Consider two identical quantum communication systems. Same satellite Same hardware Same protocol Same network architecture But located in different places. Should they perform the same? At first glance, perhaps yes. But Earth's atmosphere is far from uniform. Depending on where a ground station is located, photons may encounter very different conditions: Altitude Humidity Aerosol concentration Cloud cover Seasonal weather patterns All of these factors shape the optical channel through which quantum signals travel. This leads to a fascinating question: Can geography itself become a strategic resource for future quantum communication infrastructure? In other words, could choosing the right location provide a larger advantage than making incremental improvements to the hardware? It's a question that sits at the intersection of physics, atmospheric science, and network engineering and one I've been exploring while preparing an upcoming research manuscript. Sometimes the most important system parameter isn't built by engineers. It's provided by nature. What do you think? t: The theory of QKD is moving faster than its tooling
x: Protocols and proofs are advancing quickly, but the tools to simulate, reproduce and extend them are still fragmented. A note on what is missing. [qkd, simulation, open-source, research-tools] One thing I’ve slowly realized while exploring quantum communication and QKD research is that the theory side of the field is progressing much faster than the tooling ecosystem around it. We already have: Beautiful protocols Strong security proofs Satellite QKD demonstrations Free space optical research Attack models Quantum network architectures But when it comes to actually experimenting, simulating, reproducing, or extending these systems computationally, things still feel very fragmented. A lot of implementations are: paper specific, hard to extend, minimally documented, or abandoned after publication. And honestly, once realistic conditions enter the picture like turbulence, detector imperfections, atmospheric losses, pointing errors, and attack aware simulations, the gap becomes even more visible. Sometimes it feels like researchers spend almost as much time rebuilding infrastructure as they do exploring new ideas. There are good tools in the ecosystem already, and many researchers have built genuinely impressive simulators and frameworks over the years. But it still feels like there’s room for something more modular, reusable, physics aware, and easier to build upon collaboratively. Especially as quantum communication slowly moves from theory heavy demonstrations toward scalable real world systems.
